names.casaSub: Douglas y Agua Prieta · dos pueblos, una plaza

zone: Border market square: portales, the kiosco, antojitos and crafts

plaza.k: Douglas and Agua Prieta · the border market square
plaza.p: Two towns sit side by side on the line, Douglas in Arizona and Agua Prieta in Sonora, and they have always shared a plaza life: family on both sides, the same food, the same music on a Sunday evening. This square is built the way those plazas are: arcaded portales of cantera stone with the market stalls behind them, a bandstand in the middle, a fountain, shade trees and benches, and the food row where the smell of the trompo reaches the whole square. Walk the portales for the crafts, order at any counter, and stay for the trio after dark.

kiosco.k: The bandstand · a norteno trio plays from morning until late
kiosco.p: Almost every Mexican town square has one: an iron bandstand at the centre, where a band played on Sunday evenings while families walked around the plaza. This one is cast iron on a cantera base with talavera tile, a bell dome and a little lantern. The trio plays accordion, bajo sexto and tololoche, the upright bass of the north. Climb the steps while they play.

fountain.k: Talavera and cantera · a small fountain on the west axis
fountain.p: An octagonal basin faced with hand-painted tile, a cantera pedestal with two bowls, the water spilling from one to the next. A fountain like this was the town's meeting point before it was decoration. Sit on the rim: everyone does.

mural.t: El mural de los dos pueblos
mural.k: Casa de la Cultura · Two towns under one sky
mural.p: The mural tells the story of the two towns in one picture: the plaza with its kiosco and papel picado, families and musicians, the mountains behind, the smelter chimney of the copper years in the distance, and a biplane over it all, for the airfield that opened here in 1928 as one of the first international airports in the United States. Painted in the muralist style, in ochre, terracotta, turquoise and sage.

gateway.k: The gateway to Silver Street and Nugget Lane
gateway.p: The middle bay of the Portal Oriente opens through the building to the street: a vaulted passage, a cantera surround and a bell gable on top. Stand in the arch and look straight down Nugget Lane to Main Street, or turn round for the kiosco.

talavera.p: Talavera is tin-glazed earthenware from the Puebla region, painted by hand in cobalt blue, yellow, orange and green over a milky white glaze. Plates, jars, tiles, the big covered jars for water. The tiles on the benches and the fountain in this plaza are the same work.

hojalata.k: Tinwork · lanterns, stars and mirror frames
hojalata.p: Hojalata is tin, cut, punched and soldered into lanterns, stars, hearts and mirror frames, some of them painted. At night the punched lanterns throw patterns of light on the walls, which is why every bay of the portales has one.

pinatas.p: The classic piñata is a star with seven points and long paper fringes. The traditional reading is that each point is one of the seven sins and breaking it, blindfolded, is the reward. Today it is simply the best part of a birthday.

juguetes.t: Juguetes de madera y de trapo
juguetes.p: Painted wooden yo-yos, spinning tops, the cup and ball, little guitars, rag dolls with ribbons in their hair: the toys every grandparent on both sides of the line remembers.

flores.p: In October the flower stall fills with cempasúchil, the orange marigolds that go on the altars for Día de Muertos at the start of November, with the small white nube and the deep red cockscomb beside them.

chiles.k: Ristras, dried chiles, beans and spices
chiles.p: Strings of dried red chiles hang from the beams: ristras keep the chiles dry and they are beautiful. Below them, sacks of beans, oregano, cumin, dried chiltepin and the dark red chile for the pozole.

velas.p: Tall candles and short ones, plain wax and painted. They burn on the home altars, at the chapel and on the graves at the start of November. The stall glows at night.

barro.p: Unglazed and glazed clay: the cántaro that keeps water cool, the olla for beans and for cafe de olla, the comal for tortillas. Red clay, the colour of the ground here.

bosque.p: A step down from the square, a grove of mesquite, palo verde and desert willow on decomposed granite, with picnic tables in the shade. Bring a plate from the food row.

beto.t: Al pastor is pork marinated in chiles and achiote, stacked on the trompo and cooked by the fire behind it. I slice it straight onto the tortilla and catch a sliver of pineapple from the top. The vertical spit came with the Lebanese families who settled in Puebla; the chile is all ours.
Five is an orden. One is a taste. With onion, cilantro and the salsa verde, and a squeeze of lime.

paty.t: Elote on the stick or esquites in a cup, the same corn. Mayonesa, queso, chile and lime. In Sonora we say con todo, with everything.

cuca.t: Horchata is rice and cinnamon, jamaica is the hibiscus flower, tamarindo is sweet and sour. I make them every morning in the vitroleros, the big glass jars, so you can see what you are getting.

chema.t: The dough goes through the star nozzle straight into the hot oil, then into the cinnamon sugar. The filled ones have cajeta inside, goat milk caramel. Eat them while they are hot.

rosario.t: The conchas came out of the oven at six this morning. The pink and the yellow are vanilla, the brown is chocolate. The orejas, the marranitos, the empanadas of pumpkin. A concha with cafe de olla is how this town starts the day.
El Mirador, the lookout. My grandfather built the bakery and then the little tower on top, to see the whole plaza and the mountains. The weathervane is a biplane, for the airfield.

ramon.t: Sarapes are the striped blankets of Saltillo, woven on a loom, the stripes as bright as the weaver wants. I have scarves woven the same way, and the red paliacate, the bandana everyone ties at the neck.

lalo.t: Accordion, bajo sexto and the tololoche: the norteno trio, the music of the north of Mexico and of this border. We play from half past nine in the morning until late at night. Come up the steps and listen.
This next one is for the two towns. ¡Ajúa!

nacho.t: The bajo sexto has twelve strings in six pairs. It carries the bass line and the rhythm while the accordion sings.

tono.t: The tololoche is the upright bass. In the old days it was all a trio needed to fill the plaza, no speakers at all.

plaza: One more walk round the square?
My grandmother lived on the other side, in Agua Prieta.
The kiosco looks better every year.
food: The horchata here is the best on the line.
I came for an elote and stayed for churros.
crafts: Look at the blue on this one.
My grandmother had a sarape just like that.
mural: And the biplane over the smelter.
